Fifteen years at Westbrook High. I started as a chemistry teacher who thought my job was to prevent mistakes. I'm ending this chapter knowing it's to make them useful.

The biggest teacher in that journey wasn't my classroom. It was the after-school robotics club.

Our first competition, our robot drove straight off the table. Eleven seconds. Months of work, gone. The students stared at the floor, and I realized I had no speech ready, because in my lab, failure meant a bad grade.

In robotics, failure is data.

One student picked up the robot, looked at the wiring, and said, "Okay, so what did it tell us?" That question changed how I teach.

Now my chemistry students write down what went wrong before they write down what went right. Failed titrations get celebrated. Unexpected precipitates get investigated, not erased.

I've watched teenagers who were terrified of being wrong become people who say, "Let's find out why."

Fifteen years in, that's the reaction I'm proudest of catalyzing.

To my students, past and present: thank you for letting me learn alongside you.

What did failure teach you?
